topic: 学术综合任务与转段检查
grammarFocus: 根据个人错题复查时态、从句、冠词、数量和主谓一致。
title: The Campus Archive Digitisation Project: A Mid-Project Review
instructions: 本材料为模拟学术英语听力练习，非官方雅思试题，也不对应任何官方分数。请听四段录音（每段播放两遍），完成第1–40题。所有填空题答案必须来自录音原文，且不超过规定词数。选择题请选择最符合原文的选项。True/False/Not Given 题中，True 表示原文明确支持，False 表示原文明确矛盾，Not Given 表示原文未提供足够信息。请用中文理解解释，但答案必须用英文。
transcript:
Section 1: Social Dialogue

Man: Hi, I'm calling about the archive digitisation project. I'm a postgraduate student in history, and I'd like to know if I can access some of the digitised materials for my dissertation.

Woman: Of course. Can I take your name and student number first?

Man: Yes, it's Daniel Foster, and my student number is 2045783.

Woman: Thank you, Daniel. So, which collections are you interested in?

Man: I'm particularly interested in the papers of the first Vice-Chancellor, Sir John Marston. I understand they've been digitised.

Woman: Yes, they have. The Marston papers were part of the first phase of the project. But I should mention that some items are restricted due to data protection. The personal correspondence from the 1920s is available, but the medical records are not.

Man: That's fine. I'm mainly interested in his correspondence about the university's founding.

Woman: Good. You can access the digitised images through our online catalogue. You'll need to create an account first. Have you used the catalogue before?

Man: No, I haven't. Is it complicated?

Woman: Not really. You just need to register with your university email address, and then you can search by name, date, or subject. You can also download images for personal research use, but you can't publish them without permission.

Man: I see. And is there a limit on how many images I can download?

Woman: Yes, there is a limit of 200 images per month for postgraduate students. If you need more, you can apply for an extension.

Man: OK, that should be enough for now. One more thing: can I visit the archive in person to see the originals?

Woman: Yes, you can. The reading room is open Monday to Friday, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. You'll need to book an appointment at least two days in advance. And you'll need to bring your student card.

Man: Great. Thank you for your help.

Woman: You're welcome. Good luck with your dissertation.

Section 2: Social Monologue

Speaker: Welcome to the Northfield University Archive. This short guide will tell you what you need to know before your first visit. The archive is located in the Hartley Building, which is on the eastern edge of the campus, next to the botanical gardens. If you're coming by bus, take the number 14 or the number 22 and get off at the stop called 'University East'. From there, it's a five-minute walk.

When you arrive, please come to the reception desk on the ground floor. You'll be asked to sign in and show some form of identification. A student card or a driving licence is fine. You'll also be asked to leave your coat and bag in a locker, which is free of charge. You can bring a pencil and paper into the reading room, but pens are not allowed, and you cannot bring food or drink.

The reading room is on the first floor. It has space for up to twenty researchers at a time. You don't need to book a seat, but if you want to use one of the specialist scanners, you should reserve it in advance. The scanners are free to use, but there is a charge for printing: ten pence per page for black and white, and twenty pence for colour.

If you need help finding materials, please ask a member of staff. We're always happy to help, but we're a small team, so please be patient during busy periods. The archive is usually busiest in the mornings, so if you prefer a quieter environment, come in the afternoon.

Finally, a word about handling documents. You must wash your hands before handling any original material, and you should use the foam supports provided for bound volumes. Never place a document flat on the desk without support, and never write on top of a document. If you notice any damage, please report it to a member of staff immediately. We want to preserve these materials for future generations, and your cooperation is essential.

Thank you for listening, and we look forward to welcoming you to the archive.

Section 3: Academic Discussion

Tutor: OK, let's begin. Today we're going to discuss the case study of the Northfield Archive Digitisation Project. I'd like you to think about the challenges the project faced and what lessons can be drawn. Maria, what struck you most about the project?

Maria: I think the most interesting thing was the metadata issue. The project team estimated that cataloguing would take about 20% of the time, but it actually took nearly 40%. That's a huge difference.

Tutor: Yes, that's a good point. Why do you think they underestimated it?

Maria: Well, the text says the existing catalogue was incomplete and sometimes inaccurate. So the metadata specialist had to check each item against other sources. That must have been very time-consuming.

Tutor: Exactly. And what about the selection process? James, you looked at that, didn't you?

James: Yes. I found it interesting that the selection was controversial. Some users complained that their favourite collections were being ignored. But the project team argued that the selection was based on clear criteria.

Tutor: What were those criteria?

James: They prioritised items that were both fragile and in high demand. So some popular but robust items were deferred, and some fragile but rarely requested items were included because of their preservation needs.

Tutor: Good. Now, what about the impact of the pandemic?

Maria: The project was delayed by about six months because imaging work couldn't be done remotely. That seems like a significant setback.

Tutor: Yes, but did the project still achieve its objectives?

James: Mostly. By the end of 2021, over 11,000 items had been digitised, which was about 92% of the target. And the online catalogue was launched in October 2021.

Tutor: So would you say the project was a success?

Maria: I think so, but with some caveats. The metadata took longer than expected, and two items had to be excluded because of copyright issues. So there were some failures.

Tutor: That's a balanced view. Now, let's think about the lessons for future projects. What would you do differently?

James: I would plan more time for metadata and copyright clearance from the beginning. The project manager said that was a key lesson.

Maria: I agree. And I think it's important to involve the conservator at every stage, not just at the beginning. The case study mentions that the conservator was involved throughout.

Tutor: Good. Let's move on to consider how these lessons might apply to the second phase of the project.

Section 4: Academic Lecture

Lecturer: Good morning. Today's lecture is about the principles of digitisation, and I'll be drawing on the case study of the Northfield Archive Digitisation Project, which you should have read about. I want to focus on four key areas: selection, imaging, metadata, and preservation. These are the four pillars of any digitisation project, and if any one of them is weak, the whole project suffers.

Let's start with selection. Selection is often seen as a simple matter of choosing what to digitise, but in practice it's a complex balancing act. You have to consider the fragility of the original, the demand from users, and the legal restrictions. Sometimes these factors conflict. For example, a document might be extremely fragile and therefore a high priority for preservation, but if it's also subject to copyright, you may not be able to put it online. So you have to make difficult choices. The Northfield project prioritised items that were both fragile and in high demand, but even that criterion led to complaints from some users.

Next, imaging. The quality of the digital image is crucial. A low-resolution scan might be fine for someone who just wants to read the text, but it won't be adequate for a researcher who needs to examine handwriting or paper texture. So imaging standards must be matched to the purpose of the project. High-end projects may use specialised equipment, but smaller projects can use good-quality digital cameras. What matters most is consistency and careful handling of the original.

Now, metadata. This is the information that describes the image: who created the document, when, what it's about, and so on. Without metadata, a digital image is almost useless because no one can find it. Metadata creation is often the most time-consuming part of a project, and it's frequently underestimated. In the Northfield project, metadata took nearly 40% of the time, compared with an estimate of 20%. That's a valuable lesson.

Finally, preservation. This applies to both the original and the digital file. The original must be protected during scanning, and the digital file must be preserved for the long term. Digital storage is not permanent: files can become corrupted, formats can become obsolete, and storage media can fail. So you need a digital preservation plan, including backups and regular checks.

To conclude, digitisation is not just about taking photographs. It's about creating a resource that people can actually use. And that requires careful planning in all four areas. Thank you. I'll take questions now.

grammar.title: 时态、从句、冠词、数量与主谓一致复习
grammar.explanation: 本部分针对错题复查中常见的语法点：1) 时态：注意过去完成时（had + 过去分词）表示过去某一时间之前完成的动作；2) 从句：定语从句中关系代词的选择（which/that/who）；3) 冠词：定冠词 the 表示特指，不定冠词 a/an 表示泛指；4) 数量：可数名词复数与不可数名词的搭配；5) 主谓一致：主语为单数时谓语用单数，注意集合名词（team）可作单数或复数。
grammar.example: By 2020, over 200,000 images had been created, covering approximately 15% of the total collection.

questions.prompt: By the time the project ended, the team ______ over 11,000 items.
questions.explanation: “By the time the project ended”表示过去某一时间点之前完成的动作，用过去完成时。
questions.evidence: By the end of 2021, over 11,000 items had been digitised.

questions.prompt: The archivist, ______ had worked at the university for thirty years, retired last month.
questions.explanation: 先行词 the archivist 指人，在定语从句中作主语，用 who。
questions.evidence: The committee's first act was to appoint a part-time archivist, a former librarian named Thomas Wren.

questions.prompt: ______ archive that nobody can use is just a very expensive cupboard.
questions.explanation: archive 以元音音素开头，表示泛指“一个档案”，用不定冠词 an。
questions.evidence: 'An archive that nobody can use,' she has said, 'is just a very expensive cupboard.'

questions.prompt: The project team ______ working remotely for several months during the pandemic.
questions.explanation: team 作为集合名词，此处视为一个整体，谓语用单数 was；且描述过去事件。
questions.evidence: One was the COVID-19 pandemic, which forced the team to work remotely for several months.
